reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / WHO / India national programmes
clinicalPearls: A systemic protozoal infection caused by Leishmania donovani, transmitted by the bite of female phlebotomine sandflies
In India it is concentrated in Bihar and adjoining eastern states and is the target of a national elimination programme, with humans the main reservoir for the Indian form
Classic presentation is prolonged fever with progressive splenomegaly (often massive), hepatomegaly, weight loss, and darkening of the skin that gives the disease its name
Laboratory hallmarks are pancytopenia and a marked polyclonal hypergammaglobulinaemia
Untreated visceral leishmaniasis is almost uniformly fatal, and secondary bacterial infections and bleeding are common causes of death
Post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis can appear after apparent cure and acts as a human reservoir, so its recognition is important for elimination efforts
Diagnosis combines serology (e.g. rK39 rapid test) with demonstration of amastigotes in splenic, bone marrow or other aspirates
Effective antileishmanial therapy exists, with liposomal amphotericin B favoured in India; HIV co-infection worsens response and relapse risk
reference.pathophysiology: Sandfly bites inoculate Leishmania promastigotes, which are taken up by macrophages and transform into amastigotes that multiply within the mononuclear phagocyte system. The parasite disseminates to the spleen, liver and bone marrow, driving reticuloendothelial hyperplasia that produces organomegaly and, through hypersplenism and marrow infiltration, the characteristic pancytopenia. A vigorous but non-protective humoral response causes hypergammaglobulinaemia, while impaired cell-mediated immunity permits unchecked parasite proliferation and progressive, potentially fatal systemic disease.
additionalDifferentials: Chronic myeloproliferative disorders causing massive splenomegaly
Infective endocarditis or other causes of prolonged fever with organomegaly
infectionMimics: Lymphoma or leukaemia with organomegaly and cytopenias
additionalInvestigations: rK39 rapid serological test for L. donovani
Demonstration of amastigotes in bone marrow, splenic or lymph node aspirates
Full blood count showing pancytopenia and protein electrophoresis showing hypergammaglobulinaemia
HIV testing given the impact of co-infection on treatment and relapse
redFlags: Prolonged fever with massive splenomegaly and pancytopenia requiring urgent diagnosis and treatment
Severe anaemia, bleeding or intercurrent bacterial infection from marrow suppression, which can be fatal
Failure to respond to therapy or relapse, especially with HIV co-infection
Emergence of post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis, signalling a transmission reservoir
reference.prognosis: With prompt, effective antileishmanial therapy most patients recover fully, and liposomal amphotericin B has markedly improved outcomes in India. Untreated disease is nearly always fatal, and prognosis is poorer in the very young, malnourished, and those with HIV co-infection or advanced disease.
pitfalls: Attributing prolonged fever with splenomegaly to malaria or typhoid and missing visceral leishmaniasis in endemic areas
Overlooking HIV co-infection, which alters treatment response and relapse risk
Failing to recognise post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis as a source of ongoing transmission
Delaying treatment while awaiting invasive confirmation when serology and clinical picture are diagnostic
